summary: The 'German Christians' (Deutsche Christen) were a pro-Nazi movement within the German Protestant churches in the 1930s that sought to align Christianity with National Socialist ideology. Its programme included support for the so-called Aryan Paragraph in the church, the rejection of the Old Testament and of elements it regarded as 'Jewish,' and the pursuit of a Germanized, racially defined Christianity; the Confessing Church and the Barmen Declaration (1934) arose in opposition to its claims.
description:
The 'German Christians' (Deutsche Christen) were a movement within German Protestantism that, after Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933, sought to align the Protestant churches with National Socialist ideology and to reorganize the German Evangelical Church along Nazi lines. Emerging from earlier nationalist and voelkisch currents and organized as a church-political movement (the Faith Movement of German Christians, Glaubensbewegung Deutsche Christen), the German Christians won the church elections of July 1933 in most regional churches and pressed for the Gleichschaltung, the bringing-into-line, of the church with the new state, including the election of Ludwig Mueller as Reich Bishop.

According to the scholarly account of the movement, its programme combined several elements. It supported the introduction into the church of the so-called Aryan Paragraph, the measure that would have excluded clergy and officials of Jewish descent from church office, mirroring the racial legislation of the state. It sought to purge Christianity of what it regarded as 'Jewish' elements: prominent German Christians rejected the Old Testament, questioned or denied the Jewish ancestry of Jesus, and called for the removal of Hebrew-derived words and of hymns and texts they considered un-German. It promoted a Germanized, racially and nationally defined Christianity, in which loyalty to Volk, race, and the Fuehrer was fused with Christian profession. Historians describe the movement not as a marginal fringe but as a mass movement claiming hundreds of thousands of adherents, whose members held significant positions within the Protestant church, and note that after 1945 many of them were reintegrated into mainstream church life.

The German Christians' programme was contested from within German Protestantism. The Pastors' Emergency League (Pfarrernotbund) under Martin Niemoeller and then the wider Confessing Church (Bekennende Kirche) formed in opposition to it, and the Theological Declaration of Barmen, adopted at the first Confessing Synod in May 1934 and drafted principally by Karl Barth, rejected the claim that the church could recognize, alongside the one Word of God attested in Scripture, 'other events, powers, historic figures and truths as God's revelation.' Barmen did not name the German Christians in its text, but it was directed against their theological claims, and the confrontation between the two is the central axis of what is called the church struggle (Kirchenkampf). This entry records the German Christians' positions and programme as the historical positions of that movement, attributed to it, and records the Confessing Church's and Barmen's rejection of those claims as the historical fact it is, without adjudicating the theological questions in dispute.
editorial_notes:
NEUTRALITY: this entry presents the German Christian movement factually and historically, as what the movement held and did, attributed to it, and in a neutral register (neutrality #1, #2, #4). It does not editorialize, moralize, or adopt a devotional or polemical voice, and it does not soften the historical record. The movement's support for the Aryan Paragraph in the church, its rejection of the Old Testament and of elements it regarded as 'Jewish,' its questioning of the Jewish ancestry of Jesus, and its pursuit of a Germanized, racially defined Christianity are stated as the movement's own positions on the authority of the cited scholarship, not as the editor's characterization and not with added condemnation. Equally, the entry does not suppress the record: that the Confessing Church and the Barmen Declaration arose in opposition to the German Christians, and that Barmen rejected their theological claims, is uncontroversial historical fact and is reported as such (neutrality #5, transparency over false objectivity). The theological questions internal to German Protestantism are not adjudicated; the editor records the dispute and its participants, and does not rule on who was right.

HONESTY / status and confidence: this entry is DRAFT and, on the sourcing available, tops out at REVIEWED rather than verified. It rests on secondary historical scholarship: the German Christians' own publications and archival record are documented here through scholarly studies rather than through a directly read open primary edition, so no open German-Christian primary is claimed and none is invented. The two academic-historical studies, Doris L. Bergen, Twisted Cross: The German Christian Movement in the Third Reich (University of North Carolina Press, 1996), and Robert P. Ericksen, Theologians under Hitler (Yale University Press, 1985), are verified to exist and be on-topic but were not read line-by-line; they are rated MEDIUM. One genuinely open primary bearing on the opposition context, the Barmen Declaration (1934), was read directly and is rated HIGH; it is cited for the Confessing Church's rejection of the German Christians' theological claims, not as a source for the movement's own programme, which rests on the secondary studies. Because the movement's own positions rest on secondary scholarship rather than a directly read open primary edition of the German Christians' texts, verified status is not claimed.

The three Christian lenses (neutrality #8): (a) academic historians of the church struggle (Bergen; Ericksen); (b) the primary corpus for the opposition context, the Barmen Declaration (1934), read directly, with the German Christians' own record documented via the scholarly editions; (c) the contemporary-scholarly voice is carried by Bergen (1996) as a current historian of the movement. No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources.

Dates: the movement's decisive public emergence is placed 1932-1933 (organization as a church-political movement and the church elections of July 1933). No active_until is asserted as a clean terminus: organized German Christian activity declined after the mid-1930s and the defeat of 1945, but the entry does not fix a single end year.

No active_until is asserted: organized German Christian activity declined after the mid-1930s and after 1945, but the entry does not fix a single terminal year. Dates are approximate.

sources.citation: Bergen, Doris L. Twisted Cross: The German Christian Movement in the Third Reich. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1996 (ISBN 9780807845608). The standard English-language scholarly study of the German Christian movement, documenting its programme (support for the Aryan Paragraph in the church, rejection of the Old Testament and of 'Jewish' elements, denial of the Jewish ancestry of Jesus, the pursuit of a Germanized racial Christianity), its mass character and its members' positions within the church, and their reintegration after 1945; the primary documentary record of the movement is documented through this study. Cited as the principal academic-historical lens. Verified to exist and be on-topic (University of North Carolina Press; H-Net review by John A. Moses), not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Ericksen, Robert P. Theologians under Hitler: Gerhard Kittel, Paul Althaus, and Emanuel Hirsch. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1985 (ISBN 9780300038897). A scholarly study of three prominent Protestant theologians who supported the National Socialist regime, documenting the intellectual and theological currents that predisposed parts of German Protestantism, including the German Christian movement, toward accommodation with Nazism; cited as a second academic-historical lens on the movement's context and theology. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Yale University Press), not read line-by-line.

The Theological Declaration of Barmen, 1934. English translation, Thesis 1 and its rejection clause, confessing 'Jesus Christ, as he is attested to us in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God whom we have to hear, and whom we have to trust and obey in life and in death,' and rejecting the false doctrine that the Church could recognize 'other events, powers, historic figures and truths as God's revelation' alongside the one Word of God. Read directly for this entry. The founding confession of the Confessing Church, drafted principally by Karl Barth and directed against the German Christians' theological claims; cited as the open primary for the opposition context, not as a source for the German Christians' own programme.
